tagline.text: A short limestone cave at the site of the 1900 battle that Filipino fighters won

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay Bayanga, Cagayan de Oro, along the Cagayan de Oro–Bukidnon national highway

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱0~200 (free entry; per person including flashlight, transport and snacks)

children.text: Macahambus Cave is a short cave about 57 m long beside the national highway, roughly 15 km south of downtown Cagayan de Oro. It is the historic ground of the Battle of Macahambus Hill, fought in June 1900 during the Philippine-American War, and a balcony at the far end of the cave overlooks the Cagayan River.
Macahambus Cave sits beside the Cagayan de Oro–Airport–Bukidnon highway,
about 15 km

south of downtown Cagayan de Oro. Administratively it belongs to Barangay Bayanga, and it lies inside the 175-hectare Macahambus Forest Nature Reserve. The cave itself is a small through-cave about 57 m long: you walk down a staircase from the entrance and go in one direction to an exit on the cliff side. Think of it not as a major caving destination but as a light stop that combines a historic site, a short cave experience and a river view.

The place is famous because of the Battle of Macahambus Hill on June 4, 1900. It is regarded as one of the best-known Filipino victories in Mindanao during the Philippine-American War. According to Wikipedia, the Filipino revolutionaries defending the small hilltop fort were led by Colonel Apolinar Velez and Lieutenant Cruz Taal, and they hid pit traps lined with sharpened bamboo spears under the foliage. The US 40th Infantry force that attacked the fort is said to have withdrawn after about 10 killed and 12 wounded. At the entrance, a historical marker put up by the National Historical Commission (formerly the NHI, now the NHCP) tells this story. Sources differ slightly on casualty figures, so it is better to take away that the Filipino side won rather than to rely on exact numbers.

Natural light reaches the first chamber, but the cave gets darker and the floor more slippery as you go deeper. Some stretches require stooping, and at the end there is a balcony of iron railings and wooden planks where you can look down on the winding Cagayan River. Bats live in the cave, and a cave stream is said to re-emerge at the foot of the cliff. Entry is free and the site appears on the city government's tourist-spot list, so it fits easily into a Cagayan de Oro city tour. The entrance marker also explains that revolutionaries used the cave as a hiding place during the 1900 battle. The Macahambus forest is lush tropical woodland, and the hill above the cave is said to have once held the fort that served as headquarters of the Western Mindanao Division. It is not large, but going down into the dark and coming out at an exit overlooking the river feels like a short expedition. If you bring children, hold their hands and walk slowly; it may not suit anyone afraid of the dark.

There is something you should know before you go. In March 2025 a city councilor said the cave had been neglected and was no longer tourist-friendly, and local reports pointed to poor upkeep. According to an August 2025 article, the nearby Macahambus Gorge is closed to the public for safety reasons. For that reason this guide presents the cave as a light stop at a historic site and asks you to keep expectations modest. Please check whether it is currently open, and in what condition, with the city tourism office or locals just before you go.

This is where Filipino revolutionaries defeated American forces on June 4, 1900. Reading the battle summary on the National Historical Commission marker at the entrance makes the cave much more meaningful.
You walk down the entrance staircase and go one way to an exit on the cliff side. Beginners can manage it, but some sections require stooping and the floor is slippery.

From the iron balcony at the end of the cave you can look down on the Cagayan River flowing through the forest. Many reviews say the light is lovely around sunset, but the cave becomes very dark after sundown, so plan your time with room to spare.
The cave lies inside the Macahambus Forest Nature Reserve and is known as a bat roost. When you shine a flashlight on the ceiling or walls, keep the beam gentle so you do not startle the bats.
Several reviews mention locals renting out flashlights and selling souvenirs near the entrance. One review put the flashlight rental at about ₱20, but it may change, so confirm on site.

About 200 m south of the cave is a sinkhole (doline) formed when a cave river collapsed, commonly called Macahambus Gorge. Skybridge, zipline and rappelling activities were once offered here, but according to an August 2025 article it is closed to the public for safety reasons.

blocks.title: A stop on a Cagayan de Oro city tour

children.text: It is close to downtown and free to enter, so it slots easily into a city tour or between other sights. One to two hours is enough, so you can see it in the morning and plan city activities for the afternoon without strain.

items.title: Half-day course
items.subtitle: Historical marker, cave and viewing balcony

children.text: Set out from downtown Cagayan de Oro. One source says it takes about
12 minutes
by motorbike or tricycle from the city, but allow extra time because traffic varies.
Arrive at the roadside entrance and read the account of the 1900 battle on the National Historical Commission marker. Rent a flashlight at a stall by the entrance or get your phone light ready.
Walk down the stairs and enter the cave. Pass the first chamber with its natural light, the dark stretch and the low section where you must stoop, then head out toward the exit.
Look down on the Cagayan River from the exit balcony, take photos and rest. Check the condition of the iron railings and planks, and do not let too many people onto it at once.
Return to the highway along the cliffside path or back through the cave. The gorge side may be restricted, so follow the signs.
Return to downtown for lunch and move on to your next sight.
Local reviews say the view is good around sunset, but it is safer to be out of the cave before dark. Google Maps lists opening hours as
to
, so try to finish by
if you go in the afternoon.
Several airlines fly nonstop from Manila (NAIA) to Laguindingan Airport (CGY), which serves Cagayan de Oro. Travel time and fares vary a lot by season, so check the airline apps.
From the airport you reach downtown Cagayan de Oro by bus, van or taxi. For the distance, time and fare to downtown, it is safest to confirm on site.

One option is a jeepney bound for Talakag or Lumbia, riding along the highway and getting off near the cave entrance. Routes and fares can change, so confirm with the driver before boarding that he will let you off at Macahambus Cave.
Reviews also confirm tricycles and motorcycle taxis. Bargaining is often needed, so settle whether the driver will wait for a round trip before you set off.
Search for Macahambus Cave on Google Maps or Waze and it will guide you to the roadside entrance. There are small parking areas on both sides of the road.
If you take Grab or a taxi, it can be hard to find a ride back, so it is safer to agree on a fare that includes waiting time.
The cave entrance is right beside the highway and easy to pass by. Save the location on your map beforehand.
Cagayan de Oro is warm year-round and fairly rainy. The cave floor gets more slippery after rain and the entrance stairs get wet, so the dry season is the best time to visit.

Mornings are recommended. It is cooler, your schedule is relaxed, and you can be out of the cave before dark. Some reviews say the river view is good around sunset, so if you want that, adjust your plan so that you are out before sundown.

There is hardly any noticeable lodging near the cave, so most people stay in downtown Cagayan de Oro and make a day trip. The city has many long-established hotels and lodgings near the shopping malls, so pick one that suits your plans.

It is safer to eat in town. Around the cave entrance there are only stalls selling simple drinks and souvenirs, so bring water and snacks with you. Cagayan de Oro is known as a food city, so it pairs well with a restaurant stop in town after your visit.

On the way back, a shopping mall or a seaside restaurant in town is a good place to rest. For local food, choosing a long-established place with posted prices tends to be a safer bet than chasing famous names. Buy plenty of water before the cave visit.
It is dark inside even during the day, so bring a headlamp or a strong flashlight. A phone light alone may not be enough.
The floor is slippery, so wear sneakers with good soles. Slippers and sandals are not recommended.
Some sections require stooping, so carry a light bag, and a cap or helmet helps.
Reading the account of the 1900 battle on the entrance marker first makes it easier to understand. It also helps to read some English-language material beforehand.
The roadside entrance is easy to miss, so save the location on Google Maps and tell the jeepney driver where to drop you.
Google Maps lists hours as
to
, but this may differ from reality. Check the latest notice just before you go.
Bring water and snacks, and carry your trash out. It is a bat roost, so do not make loud noises or keep shining a flash on them.
On rainy days it is better to switch to city sightseeing. The cave floor and entrance stairs are especially slippery.
In March 2025 a city councilor pointed to the cave's neglect and improper use, and the nearby gorge is closed for safety reasons. Be sure to check whether it is open before you go.
According to local reports, residents have said the cave is used for drug-related activity and improper gatherings. Do not go alone; visit in daylight with companions.
The floor is slippery and some sections have low ceilings, so there is a risk of injury. After rain, even the entrance stairs are slippery.
Some sources say steps are missing on the gorge's iron staircase, and as of August 2025 public access is closed. Do not ignore no-entry signs and go down anyway.
One review mentions a large hornet's nest near the entrance. Do not make noise or touch anything near the nest.
The balcony's iron railings and planks may be worn. Do not let many people onto it at once, and do not lean on the railing.
Downtown is about
15 km
from the cave, and all the lodging, restaurants and shopping are there. Combine it with city sightseeing for a full-day plan.
A signature highland resort of Northern Mindanao, it can be combined with a trip up toward Bukidnon from Cagayan de Oro. Check travel times locally.
A signature waterfall of northern Mindanao, but it lies in the opposite direction toward Iligan, so plan it as a separate trip. Check the distance locally.
Cagayan de Oro is famous for white-water rafting on the Cagayan River. Starting points differ by operator, so confirm when booking and ask whether trips are currently running.
